content: The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT-C) is a screening tool designed to assess alcohol consumption. It consists of three questions and can be administered using paper-and-pencil or through an interviewer. Its sensitivity ranges from 18% to 100%, and its specificity ranges from 71% to 100%, depending on the population and cut-off points used. The CAGE questionnaire is another alcohol screening tool, consisting of four questions. It is typically self-administered using paper-and-pencil and was not initially validated for use in prenatal or pregnant populations. Its sensitivity ranges from 38% to 59%, and its specificity ranges from 82% to 92%. The NET (Not Early Testing) tool is a three-question alcohol screening test that can be administered in both inpatient and outpatient settings. It is also paper-and-pencil-based, with sensitivity ranging from 24% to 71% and specificity from 86% to 99%. The Short Michigan Alcohol Screening Test (SMAST) is a 13-question tool for alcohol use assessment. It is self-administered using paper-and-pencil and has a sensitivity of 11% to 15% and a specificity of 96% to 98%. The Ten Question Drinking History (TQDH) is a 10-question alcohol screening tool administered by an interviewer. It is specifically used in prenatal clinics to assess alcohol use. The T-ACE questionnaire is a four-question alcohol screening tool designed for use in prenatal clinics. It is paper-and-pencil-based, with sensitivity ranging from 60% to 91% and specificity from 37% to 79%. The TWEAK questionnaire is a five-question alcohol screening tool also used in prenatal clinics. It is paper-and-pencil-based, with sensitivity ranging from 59% to 92% and specificity from 64% to 92%. It is important to note that the sensitivity and specificity of these tools vary depending on the cut-off points used to determine risk. Additionally, some tools were not initially developed or validated for use in pregnant populations. For example, the CAGE questionnaire was not specifically designed for prenatal use. The harmful use of alcohol and illicit drugs is the third leading risk factor for premature deaths and disabilities worldwide. In 2004, approximately 5 million people died from alcohol-related causes, including 320,000 young individuals aged 15 to 29 years. Guidelines for identifying and managing substance use and substance use disorders during pregnancy emphasize the importance of using validated tools and tailoring interventions to the specific needs of pregnant women. These guidelines are informed by contributions from experts in substance use treatment, obstetric care, and infant health, as well as those with experience in lowand middle-income settings.
